text:
I compared this file against the upstream `ms@2.1.3` source line by line.

- Helpers (`s`, `m`, `h`, `d`, `w`, `y`), the public `module.exports`, `fmtShort`, `fmtLong`, and `plural` are all verbatim identical to 2.1.3.
- The only difference is in `parse`: the original `switch` on unit names was replaced by a `multipliers` lookup table guarded by `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`.

Checking that refactor exhaustively: the regex can only produce 31 possible unit strings (`millisecond(s)`, `msec(s)`, `ms`, `second(s)`, `sec(s)`, `s`, `minute(s)`, `min(s)`, `m`, `hour(s)`, `hr(s)`, `h`, `day(s)`, `d`, `week(s)`, `w`, `year(s)`, `yr(s)`, `y`), all matched case-insensitively and then lowercased. Every one of those 31 strings is present as an own key in the `multipliers` object with the correct value (`y`/`w`/`d`/`h`/`m`/`s`/`1`). The `hasOwnProperty` guard can therefore never fire for any regex-matchable input, and when it can't match, both versions return `undefined`. Returning `n * 1` for milliseconds is numerically identical to the original `return n` (including `-0`). No prototype-pollution lookup is reachable since the regex restricts `type` to the known unit names.

So for every input — valid units in any case, unknown units, over-long strings, numbers, invalid types — the observable result is identical to 2.1.3. This is an equivalent refactor, not a defect.

```json
{"defect": false, "note": "The switch-to-lookup-table refactor in parse() is behaviorally identical: all 31 unit strings the regex can produce are present as own keys in multipliers with the correct multipliers, the hasOwnProperty guard makes the default case equivalent (undefined), and n*1 equals n for the ms case. All other functions match upstream ms@2.1.3 verbatim."}
```
